clinicalPearls: A multisystem ectodermal-mesodermal disorder in which atrophic, linear skin lesions follow the lines of Blaschko
Soft, yellow-pink outpouchings of herniated fat through the thinned dermis (fat herniation) are a characteristic cutaneous sign
Raspberry-like papillomas around the mouth, anus and vulva, and periungual/mucosal papillomas, are frequent
Skeletal defects, classically osteopathia striata on radiographs and limb anomalies such as syndactyly and 'lobster-claw' hands, are common
Ocular (colobomata, microphthalmia) and dental anomalies frequently accompany the skin findings
X-linked dominant, caused by PORCN mutations; usually lethal in males, so most patients are female and mosaicism explains survival in the few affected males
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, addressing skin, skeletal, ocular and dental problems
reference.pathophysiology: Focal dermal hypoplasia (Goltz syndrome) is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by mutations in PORCN, which encodes an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane O-acyltransferase required for the palmitoylation and secretion of WNT signalling proteins. WNT signalling is fundamental to the development of skin, bone, eyes, teeth and other structures, so its impairment produces the widespread mesoectodermal defects. The condition is generally lethal in hemizygous males; affected males who survive typically have somatic mosaicism. Random X-inactivation in females creates functional mosaicism, which accounts for the Blaschko-linear distribution of the skin lesions, where dermal connective tissue is hypoplastic and subcutaneous fat herniates through the attenuated dermis.
additionalDifferentials: MIDAS/microphthalmia with linear skin defects syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing marked dermal thinning with fat approaching the epidermis
Skeletal radiographs for osteopathia striata and limb anomalies
Ophthalmological examination for colobomata and microphthalmia
Dental assessment for enamel and tooth anomalies
redFlags: Major limb or skeletal anomaly requiring surgical management
Complications of extensive skin fragility such as infection
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the pattern and severity of extracutaneous involvement rather than the skin disease; many affected individuals have a normal lifespan. Ocular, skeletal and dental problems account for most long-term morbidity and often require ongoing multidisciplinary care.
pitfalls: Focusing on the skin lesions and failing to screen for skeletal, ocular and dental anomalies
Misinterpreting fat herniation as a benign lipomatous naevus without recognising the syndrome
Overlooking the diagnosis in a rare affected male, in whom mosaicism is expected
Not offering genetic counselling given X-linked dominant inheritance and male lethality
management: Supportive skin care with management of symptomatic or bleeding papillomas by excision, laser ablation or cryotherapy
Orthopaedic and reconstructive surgery for limb anomalies such as syndactyly and split-hand deformity
Ophthalmological assessment and management of colobomata and microphthalmia to optimise vision
Dental care for enamel and tooth anomalies
Multidisciplinary developmental and organ-system evaluation directed at the pattern of extracutaneous involvement
Genetic counselling for X-linked dominant inheritance with PORCN testing, discussion of male lethality and mosaicism, and family screening
